items.abstract: Superconductor-semiconductor coupling in hybrid nanowires plays a pivotal role in Majorana devices. Here, we demonstrate this tunable coupling in PbTe-Pb nanowires and its impact on the induced gap and zero-bias peaks (ZBPs). In the strong coupling regime, the device reveals a clean superconducting gap, where robust and non-robust ZBPs are observed in distinct magnetic field ranges. Conversely, increasing the gate voltage drives the system toward the weak coupling regime, where the gap becomes narrow and soft. Consequently, robust ZBPs disappear while non-robust ones persist. Our results establish a direct link between tunable coupling and robust ZBPs, providing guidelines on engineering Majorana zero modes and topological qubits.
items.why: Gate-tuned coupling in PbTe-Pb nanowires links robust zero-bias peaks to the strong-coupling regime.

items.title: Crosstalk-Induced Row Hammer Attacks on Quantum Random Access Codes
items.abstract: Quantum processors remain susceptible to crosstalk-induced effects despite the continuous evolution of their underlying hardware architectures. In this work, we experimentally investigate the effectiveness of crosstalk-induced attacks across six IBM superconducting quantum processors and one IQM processor. Our results demonstrate that such attacks can be launched across all the platforms, due to persistance of crosstalk, although their effectiveness varies significantly between devices. The probability of a measurement outcome flip in the victim qubits reaches a maximum value of $60\%$. Also, it is seen that processors sharing identical coupling graphs exhibit different vulnerability profiles, indicating that connectivity alone is insufficient to predict attack efficiency. Finally, to demonstrate the practical relevance of these attacks, we study their impact on quantum random access codes (QRACs), observing a degradation in their average success probabilities.
items.why: Crosstalk attacks flip victim-qubit outcomes up to 60% across six IBM and one IQM processor.

items.title: Multicopy teleportation and quantum program retrieval on superconducting quantum hardware
items.abstract: Correction-free teleportation protocols offer a probabilistic route around the limits imposed by the quantum no-programming theorem, but have remained largely theoretical. Here, we experimentally implement and benchmark correction-free multicopy teleportation on noisy superconducting quantum hardware. Key to this is an efficient circuit implementation: by suitably decomposing the unitary that maps the multicopy measurement basis onto the computational basis, we substantially reduce circuit depth and gate count. For one- and two-qubit input states, using $k=2$ and $3$ copies, we observe success probabilities substantially exceeding the single-copy bound with fidelities above 0.85. We further explore applications to probabilistic programmable quantum processors, in particular the storage and retrieval of unitary operations encoded in quantum program states. Our results establish the practical feasibility of multicopy teleportation and highlight its potential for near-term quantum processors and distributed quantum computing.
items.why: Correction-free multicopy teleportation on IBM hardware beats single-copy success with fidelities above 0.85.

items.title: Multipartite entanglement swapping with homodyne and single photon detection
items.abstract: Establishing multipartite entanglement across lossy optical networks remains a central challenge for distributed quantum information processing. Here, we consider a non-Gaussian continuous-variable entanglement-swapping protocol combining a symmetric discrete Fourier transform (DFT) interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection. In the ideal limit, single-photon heralding generates a $W_N$-class state across remote modes, with Fourier symmetry rendering all single-click outcomes equivalent up to local phase corrections. We find that conditional pairwise entanglement can exceed that of conventional Gaussian homodyne swapping in weak-to-moderate squeezing and lossy regimes, remaining nonzero beyond the channel-loss thresholds at which Gaussian pairwise entanglement vanishes. These results demonstrate that combining non-Gaussian measurements with symmetric interferometric mixing can improve both the resilience and operational efficiency of multipartite entanglement distribution in lossy quantum networks.
items.why: Fourier-interferometer swapping with photon counting beats Gaussian swapping under loss.

items.title: Classical and Quantum Dynamics in State Space: Projective Hilbert Space, Measurement, and Classical Emergence
items.abstract: We develop a geometric formulation of classical and quantum dynamics in which projective Hilbert space is taken as the primary state space and classical configuration and phase spaces arise as submanifolds of localized quantum states. The Fubini-Study metric induces the Euclidean metric on these submanifolds, while the tangential component of Schrödinger evolution reproduces Hamiltonian and Newtonian dynamics. We then extend the construction to stochastic motion. Brownian dynamics on the localized classical manifold is lifted to a common stochastic unitary evolution in projective Hilbert space; under homogeneity, isotropy, and independence assumptions, the corresponding Hermitian increments have Gaussian Unitary Ensemble statistics. This yields a random-matrix Schrödinger dynamics whose transition probabilities depend only on Fubini-Study distance. Through the embedding of localized states, the classical Gaussian transition law becomes the Born rule in projective state space. Measurement outcomes are identified with first arrival at detector-defined finite-resolution equivalence classes, while each realized state-space evolution remains linear and unitary. The framework is applied to classical emergence, macroscopic stabilization, double-slit experiments, composite systems, and entangled states. A spatially local Caldeira-Leggett-type system-environment model is also shown, under explicit thermal, symmetry, Ohmic, and coarse-graining assumptions, to generate the Brownian family required by the stochastic lift. The remaining open problem is to establish the range and universality of this mechanism for realistic many-body measuring environments.
items.why: Geometric framework derives the Born rule from Brownian motion lifted to projective Hilbert space.

eli5.plain: He builds classical physics as a slice of quantum state space and gets the Born rule from random motion.
eli5.how: Classical phase space is embedded as localised states; random-matrix Schrödinger dynamics gives transition probabilities set by Fubini-Study distance.
eli5.matters: Another attempt at deriving the Born rule rather than postulating it.
eli5.caveat: Rests on assumptions that do much of the work.

items.title: Superconducting Qubits as Quantum Targets for Direct Particle Scattering
items.abstract: We introduce a novel approach to particle detection in which a superconducting qubit itself serves as the scattering target and a resolved transition between circuit eigenstates constitutes the observable final state. The scattering amplitude factorizes into the incident-particle current and a finite-momentum electromagnetic transition response of the qubit. This momentum dependence is essential in that the energy transfer is fixed by the microwave-scale level spacing, whereas a nonrelativistic incident particle can transfer a spatial momentum parametrically larger than that energy and thereby resolve the device geometry. For charge-dominated processes, we recast the response as an induced-offset-charge kernel obtained from an auxiliary electrostatic weighting potential, providing a practical route from circuit geometry to a differential scattering cross section. We illustrate the framework with an Xmon-style transmon and photon-mediated scattering of dark matter. The exceptionally small qubit transition threshold opens sensitivity to an eV-to-keV mass regime that is largely unexplored by existing direct-detection experiments.
items.why: Treats a transmon as a scattering target, with circuit-geometry cross sections for eV-keV dark matter.

items.title: Enhanced shortcuts to adiabaticity in an interacting giant-atom-atomic-waveguide system
items.abstract: In realistic quantum systems, isolated few-level models usually provide only an approximate description, since the controlled subsystem is generally coupled to additional degrees of freedom. As a result, a quantum control scheme designed for an isolated system may lose its original performance in a more complex coupled setting. Here, we consider a giant atom coupled to an interacting atomic waveguide and investigate enhanced shortcuts to adiabaticity (eSTA) in such a structured system. As a first step, a weak-coupling perturbative analysis identifies how changes in the initial and target states, together with dynamical transitions, contribute to the fidelity loss. Starting from a shortcut to adiabaticity control scheme for the uncoupled system, the enhanced STA correction improves the final fidelity by modifying only the giant-atom control fields. This improvement is found for both periodic and open boundary conditions of the atomic waveguide. The results demonstrate a way to design an eSTA protocol for an interacting composite system.
items.why: Enhanced shortcuts to adiabaticity correct giant-atom control in an interacting atomic waveguide.

items.title: Parametric $\mathrm{CZ}$ Gates in a Tunable Tripod Architecture with Fixed-Frequency Superconducting Qubits
items.abstract: Efficient implementation of the operations required for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum computers requires high gate fidelity, adequate qubit connectivity, and selective control of interactions. Sharing a single coupler among multiple qubits can improve connectivity, but also requires accounting for its effects on qubits outside the target pair. In this work, we numerically investigate the feasibility of implementing parametric-resonance $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates in a tunable tripod structure consisting of three fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler. We modulate the external flux applied to the coupler and optimize the pulse parameters for each qubit pair to construct $\mathrm{CZ}_{01}$, $\mathrm{CZ}_{02}$, and $\mathrm{CZ}_{12}$ gates. We calculate the time evolution of a Hamiltonian that includes three energy levels for each circuit element and evaluate gate fidelity and leakage after virtual Z correction. The fidelities obtained for the target-pair computational blocks, whose input and output basis states have both the coupler and spectator qubit in their ground states, are 0.9943, 0.9834, and 0.9907, respectively. We also find that population preservation at the end of the gate depends on the initial state of the spectator qubit. These results demonstrate the possibility of constructing $\mathrm{CZ}$ operations for each qubit pair through flux modulation of a shared coupler while maintaining fixed data-qubit frequencies. They also highlight the need to evaluate performance and optimize control over the full computational space, including the spectator qubit.
items.why: Simulated parametric CZ gates between three transmons sharing one tunable coupler, with leakage analysis.

items.title: Scalable Transpilation for Overcoming Restricted Connectivity in Distributed Superconducting Quantum Architectures
items.abstract: Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) offers a promising pathway to scale superconducting quantum hardware, but restricted inter- and intra-module connectivity creates a major transpilation bottleneck. Current DQC transpilation methods often assume idealized hardware connectivity, ignore subsequent intra-module routing, or suffer from substantial computational overheads that limit their applicability at scale. To address this, we introduce a scalable transpilation method tailored for the restricted connectivity of distributed superconducting quantum architectures. Specifically, our quantum interaction graph (QIG) approach couples a graph-partitioning mapping step with a fast SABRE-inspired routing heuristic. On a 48-qubit (3 QPUs $\times$ 16 qubits) architecture with all-to-all inter-core connectivity, our method reduces average aggregated costs by up to 24.72% (unstructured) and 24.01% (structured), while delivering >250$\times$ speed-ups for structured workloads compared to the state-of-the-art DMapS algorithm. On the 399-qubit (3$\times$133) IBM Flamingo, where DMapS times out on dense circuits, our approach maintains practical runtimes. Against a DQC-adapted SABRE baseline, it reduces structured circuit routing costs by up to 51.94% (all-to-all inter-core topology) and 51.96% (restricted line topology). Ultimately, this work delivers a practical transpilation method for DQC at scale.
items.why: Graph-partitioning transpiler cuts distributed-architecture routing cost ~25% with large speed-ups over DMapS.

items.title: Colloidal 2D WS2 nanosheets exhibiting high-purity single photon emission
items.abstract: The search for quantum emitters, delivering single photons "on demand" at cryogenic and elevated temperatures for photonic technologies is ever progressing. For example, micrometer-sized WS2 monolayers exhibit single photon emission by elaborated local defect or strain engineering. Here, we show that wet-chemically synthesised monolayered two-dimensional (2D) WS2 nano sheets (NSs) with lateral sizes of 14 (+/- 6 nm) readily emit single photons from exciton recombination without the need for substrate-induced patterning, strain/defect engineering or spectral filtering. Single particle spectroscopy of 70 individual NSs shows photoluminescence from excitons (2.02 eV), trios (1.94 eV) and defect-localized states (1.85 eV) with fast emission (t1<0.2 ns, t2=3.2 ns), allowing highly frequent excitation cycles. Pulsed at 80 MHz, colloidal WS2 NSs exhibit limited spectral diffusion, no blinking and distinct photon antibunching (g2(0)=0.07 at 5 K), thereby tackling challenges of established colloidal quantum dot systems (blinking, longer emission cycles), while retaining high single photon purity as key quality of deterministic quantum emitters.
items.why: Colloidal WS2 nanosheets emit single photons with g2(0)=0.07 and no blinking.

items.title: Semi-classical analysis of noise squeezing in Kerr microresonators
items.abstract: Kerr microresonators are integrated nonlinear devices widely used to generate classical optical frequency combs and nonclassical states of light. In particular, they provide a promising platform for squeezed light sources, which are important elements of emerging quantum sensing, communication, and computing technologies. Designing such sources requires numerical tools that efficiently incorporate realistic device physics and noise processes. Here, we show that established semi-classical frameworks based on the Lugiato-Lefever equation and the Ikeda map, instrumental in the development of classical light sources, can also predict the quadrature-noise properties of squeezed light when vacuum fluctuations are properly included. We consider three canonical configurations producing two-mode quadrature squeezing, single-mode quadrature squeezing, and intensity difference squeezing. In each case, the semi-classical simulations produce quadrature variances and noise spectra in close agreement with the quantum theoretical predictions. These frameworks therefore provide practical tools for designing squeezed light sources, with the capability to incorporate additional noise mechanisms, nonlinear effects, and complex resonator arrangements. More fundamentally, our results show that key experimental signatures of squeezing can be modeled as phase-sensitive amplification of properly normalized vacuum fluctuations within stochastic semi-classical field equations. This observation helps distinguish squeezing properties accessible through semi-classical field evolution from those intrinsically requiring a full quantum description.
items.why: Lugiato-Lefever and Ikeda-map simulations with vacuum noise reproduce Kerr microresonator squeezing.

items.title: Polyteam logics for quantum contextuality
items.abstract: We introduce logics of dependence and independence over polyteams (that is, databases with multiple relation schemes), in a similar way as in arXiv:1704.02158v3 [cs.LO]. On this basis, we develop a logical framework in which we can express (in formulas) relevant properties about the statistics of a repeated quantum experiment. In this framework, we formalize Bell's theorem, and the Kochen-Specker theorem as failure of logical entailments, as it was suggested in arXiv:2107.10817v3 [math.LO]. The key feature of polyteam logics in action here is their power to express both local and global properties, with respect to the set of possible measurements. The point of this is at least twofold. Firstly, as in arXiv:1102.0264v7 [quant-ph], it gives a high-level (information-theoretic) understanding of these physical phenomena, that is not intrinsic to the physical objects involved. Secondly, since logical entailment is often (partially) axiomatizable, this framework incites us to tackle the question of contextuality computationally. We also define semiring-weighted polyteams along with logics on them, and use them to recover the probabilistic versions of the contextuality theorems mentioned above.
items.why: Polyteam dependence logics recast Bell and Kochen-Specker as failures of logical entailment.

eli5.plain: She writes contextuality theorems in a logic for databases.
eli5.how: Polyteams capture local and global measurement statistics, so Bell and KS become entailments that fail.
eli5.matters: Could make contextuality checks computable.
eli5.caveat: Mainly formalism; no new physical claim.

items.title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
items.abstract: We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.
items.why: Iterative KAM-based DRAG restores two-level robust pulses while suppressing multilevel leakage.

items.title: Finite-Time Thermodynamic Routing in an Anharmonic Collective Quantum Otto Engine
items.abstract: The Gibbs state determined by a thermal reservoir does not determine how a working medium approaches it or how fluctuations accumulate over repeated cycles. We exploit this kinetic freedom in an anharmonic collective quantum Otto engine. A longitudinal interaction separates neighboring Dicke transition frequencies without changing their collective matrix elements, allowing passive spectral shaping to route finite-time transport among edges with different heat costs while preserving the contact Gibbs states. Exact edge-current identities and repeated-cycle counting statistics link this routing to mean work, hot heat, and intercycle work correlations. At fixed thermal-contact exposure, structured reservoirs can increase both mean work and long-time squared precision; equal-work controls distinguish these gains from uniform relaxation-rate changes. The useful regime is mesoscopic, bounded by spectral resolution and physical contact time. An equal-cooling example and a full-spin local-noise study test the mechanism beyond ideal engine operation, the latter retaining a one-cycle precision gain despite spin-sector mixing. In a six-transmon dressed-spectrum model, passive microwave filters at fixed integrated coupling achieve equal mean work with shorter thermal contacts, corresponding to higher contact-time-normalized output, and with long-time squared precision comparable to that of the fastest sampled flat reference. The transition pathways selected by a passive reservoir thus provide a control variable for finite-time performance and accumulated work fluctuations that is independent of thermal equilibrium.
items.why: Spectral shaping of Dicke transitions routes finite-time heat flow in a collective quantum Otto engine, raising work and precision.

items.title: Resonance-engineered single-photon routing in an asymmetric Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide system
items.abstract: We investigate single-photon scattering and routing in an asymmetric cavity-waveguide quantum electrodynamics system consisting of a Jaynes-Cummings cavity-emitter subsystem coupled to two one-dimensional waveguides. Using a real-space scattering approach, we derive an exact three-channel scattering matrix and analytical expressions for the channel-resolved scattering amplitudes. The scattering response is governed by the interplay of asymmetric cavity-waveguide coupling, atom-cavity detuning, coherent preparation of a single-photon superposition across multiple input channels, and intrinsic dissipation. Coupling asymmetry controls the relative weights of the cavity-mediated scattering pathways, whereas atom-cavity detuning modifies their spectral response. Coherent multichannel input states provide an additional phase-sensitive control of the output probabilities through interference. In particular, we identify an analytical condition, $J_2=2J_1$ and $α_1=-α_2$, under which the probability in the second output channel becomes independent of photon energy; for an equal-weight normalized input, this probability is 1/2. We further show how cavity and atomic dissipation reduce the probability remaining in the guided channels. These results provide a framework for resonance-engineered single-photon routing in asymmetric Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide systems.
items.why: Exact three-channel S-matrix for asymmetric JC routing with an energy-independent output condition.

items.title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
items.abstract: Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.
items.why: Boron nitride nanotubes host room-temperature single-photon emitters across the visible range.

items.title: Spin-Exchange-Controlled Nonclassical Light in Cavity Electromagnetically Induced Transparency
items.abstract: Controlling nonclassical light while maintaining a finite cavity response requires selective suppression of unwanted multiphoton excitation. We investigate a ring-cavity system containing two three-level emitters coupled by a coherent spin-exchange interaction, where electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) provides resonant access to a dark-state polariton. The exchange interaction shifts the polariton resonance while modifying the dressed two-photon excitation pathways. Strong photon antibunching emerges when the one-polariton resonance nearly coincides with a destructive-interference minimum of the second-photon transition amplitude. By jointly tuning the exchange interaction and control-field strength, pronounced photon blockade with a finite intracavity population can be sustained over an extended interaction range. We further show that the relative cavity-coupling phase redistributes optical coupling between symmetric and antisymmetric collective channels with opposite exchange shifts, allowing the photon statistics to switch between antibunching and bunching at fixed exchange strength. This mechanism provides a possible route to tunable nonclassical-light sources based on coherent control of collective excitation pathways.
items.why: Spin exchange between emitters in cavity EIT tunes photon blockade and switches bunching to antibunching.

items.title: Quantum Simulation of Electronic Structure using Quantum Density Functional Theory on a Programmable Integrated Photonic Circuit
items.abstract: Quantum simulations of molecular electronic structure hold the potential for computational advantage but are inherently limited by the linear scaling of qubit requirements with respect to system size. Quantum Density Functional Theory (Q-DFT) addresses this constraint by reformulating the interacting many-body problem in terms of a non-interacting Kohn--Sham reference system. Here, we present and experimentally validate a Q-DFT algorithm that requires only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2(N))$ qubits to simulate a system of $N$ orbitals, thereby reducing resource overhead. More precisely, we solve the Kohn--Sham problem for the lithium hydride (LiH) molecule using the ensemble extension of the variational quantum eigensolver paradigm that minimizes the energy of the system in the subspace spanned by the ground and first excited states. To execute this task, we encode the problem with qubits on a quantum photonic platform, utilizing an architecture that combines a deterministic quantum dot single-photon source with a programmable integrated photonic circuit. By evaluating the molecular ground- and first excited-state properties, this work establishes a pathway for simulating larger molecular systems, demonstrating the viability of integrating qubit-efficient algorithms with advanced reconfigurable photonic hardware for near-term quantum chemistry applications.
items.why: Q-DFT on a quantum-dot-fed photonic chip solves LiH Kohn-Sham with log₂N qubits.

items.title: Cooling-path-selected self-assembly of telecom InAsP quantum dots
items.abstract: Epitaxial quantum dots are leading solid-state sources of quantum light, but reproducible growth on indium phosphide (InP) remains challenging because dot-formation windows are narrow and emission wavelengths are difficult to predict. Here we report a new epitaxial route for InAsP quantum dots on InP(001), in which the cooling path selects the final morphology without intentional deposition of group-III dot material. High-temperature As exposure forms a shallow near-surface InAsP layer through As-P exchange; the cooling path and continued As supply determine whether three-dimensional islands form. Surface-sensitive spectroscopy shows near-surface As enrichment, while cross-sectional STEM/EELS identifies graded, As-rich InAsP islands. The capped emitters span 1.2-1.6 micrometers, with single-photon emission observed up to 100 K. Across 20 wafers, the surface-effective exchange dose D provides a practical calibration for targeting the median emission wavelength. These results establish cooling as an active epitaxial step for telecom InAsP quantum-dot formation and wavelength control.
items.why: Cooling-path-selected growth yields telecom InAsP dots with single photons up to 100 K.

items.title: Optimal Estimation in Weak Value Amplification with a Position Pointer
items.abstract: We experimentally evaluate five estimators for weak-value amplification (WVA) using a position pointer to measure birefringence time delays. Two general approaches are considered: measuring the position shift $Δx$ and measuring the probability change $ΔP_w$ of successful postselection. Specifically, five estimators are investigated: CCD-detected fringe shift $Δx$, quadrant photodiode (PDQ) transversal voltage difference (XDIFF), and lock-in amplifier output phase $η$ (for $Δx$ measurement), as well as PDQ total output voltage (SUM) and CCD-detected average photon number $N_r$ (for $ΔP_w$ measurement). The measurement precision is characterized by the Allan deviation over a range of input laser powers $P_0$. Generally, measuring the position shift $Δx$ yields higher precision than measuring the probability change $ΔP_w$. At $P_0=0.5$~mW, corresponding to a laser-power-limited regime, direct measurement of the fringe displacement with the CCD achieves a minimum Allan deviation of $(5.30\pm0.10)\times10^{-3}$~as, approaching the corresponding photon-statistical Cramér--Rao bound (CRB). At $P_0=50$~mW, corresponding to a detector-limited regime, PDQ detection combined with lock-in demodulation provides the best precision, reaching $(1.80\pm0.06)\times10^{-3}$~as and remaining close to the corresponding CRB. These results demonstrate that the optimal readout depends on the available optical power, detector dynamic range, and technical noise, providing practical guidance for selecting readout strategies in high-precision WVA-based metrology.
items.why: Compares five weak-value-amplification estimators; CCD fringe shift approaches the Cramér-Rao bound.

items.title: Multiparameter quantum metrology for general and adaptive strategies
items.abstract: We develop a conic-programming framework for multiparameter estimation of quantum processes under different classes of sensing strategies. Estimation precision depends on the choice of input probe state and measurement and, when a channel is used multiple times, on the arrangement of channel uses and intermediate controls. We specify different strategy classes through linear normalization constraints on generalized measurements, and formulate the local estimation problem using linear constraints and a linear objective function. We show that the separable-cone program gives the exact precision limit under the local estimation conditions considered here, while cone relaxations yield Cramér-Rao-type lower bounds. For $N$ uses of an identical quantum channel, we prove an exact $1/N$ scaling law for an RLD-based positive-cone lower bound, even for general process-matrix testers that allow indefinite causal order. Under the stated conditions on the channel and its parameter dependence, the minimum weighted mean-square error also scales as $1/N$. This extends an RLD-based restriction on Heisenberg scaling from adaptive strategies to this broader class. For fixed-order adaptive strategies, we show that each process-side conic bound equals the corresponding state-estimation bound optimized over sensor combs. We establish this equality by constructing a sensor comb from the process-side normalization operator. A noisy three-parameter field-sensing model illustrates the framework.
items.why: Conic programs give exact multiparameter precision limits, with 1/N scaling even with indefinite causal order.

eli5.plain: They set exact precision limits for estimating several parameters of a quantum process.
eli5.how: Strategies become linear constraints in a conic program; an RLD bound gives 1/N scaling.
eli5.matters: Shows indefinite causal order does not beat standard scaling here.
eli5.caveat: Metrology result; foundations content is thin.

items.title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
items.abstract: Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at $n=3$ is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.5$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them ($1.8$ to $88$ times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a $10$\,mrad rms error then costs $1.2\times10^{7}$ shots in $65$\,s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while $n\ge5$ stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.
items.why: Exhaustive search finds minimal recovery-gate counts for repetition-code process tomography at n=3,5,7.

items.title: Cooperative Suppression of Two-Particle Excitation by Kerr Nonlinearity and Cavity Loss ion a Driven Holstein-Tavis-Cumming System
items.abstract: We apply the numerically accurate multiple Davydov Ansatz (multi-$\rm D_2$) method to investigate the nonequilibrium dynamics of an open molecular cavity system using an extended driven-dissipative Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model incorporating Kerr nonlinearity. Our results reveal that the synergy between Kerr nonlinearity and exciton-phonon coupling induces an anharmonic level structure, imposing a stringent energy penalty that isolates the one-excitation manifold. This establishes a robust single-excitation-dominated regime that dynamically manifests photon blockade, characterized by suppression of the pure two-photon state and isolation of the one-excitation manifold. While strong coherent driving induces power broadening that overcomes the nonlinear barrier and opens multiphoton channels, cavity dissipation counteracts this process by acting as a highly selective manifold filter. By preferentially depleting fragile multi-photon states while sheltering single excitations within dissipation-free dark states, the cavity mode decay rate actively cooperates with Kerr nonlinearity to restore and reinforce the photon blockade effect. These findings elucidate the intricate interplay among nonlinearity, driving, and dissipation, offering a theoretical blueprint for engineering robust single-photon sources in open molecular cavity platforms.
items.why: Kerr nonlinearity and cavity loss jointly isolate the one-excitation manifold in a molecular cavity.

items.title: Noise-Induced Topology in Chiral Quantum Walks
items.abstract: Noise typically destroys quantum coherence and washes out transport phenomena that rely on interference. Chiral quantum walks are a case in point: a particle hopping on a lattice threaded by a magnetic flux can spread asymmetrically due to interference between paths, an asymmetry that noise is expected to erase. Remarkably, we find that the most ubiquitous noise -- random fluctuations of on-site energies (dephasing) -- instead renders this asymmetry topologically robust. The density profile develops a skewness that grows in time while its center stays fixed, and in a finite chain the late-time relaxation modes pile up at one edge: a skin effect lacking the drift of conventional non-Hermitian skin effects. With multiple sites per unit cell, the dephasing strength alone can cause a topological phase transition, reversing the asymmetry. On a flux ladder with noisy rung hopping, the noise causes a drift of rung coherences, a quantum ratchet with no classical counterpart. Underlying these effects, the noise-averaged dynamics is an interacting (generically non-integrable) Lindbladian that remains analytically tractable. The modes governing late-time relaxation are bound states of the noise-induced interaction and form a band with a point gap, absent both without noise and under postselection, whose winding number fixes the direction of the asymmetry. These effects are within reach of several experimental platforms, including synthetic lattices, superconducting qubits, and optical lattices.
items.why: On-site dephasing makes chiral quantum-walk asymmetry topological, with a drift-free skin effect.

items.title: A Phase-Balanced Differential Rydberg-Atom Quantum Receiver for Weak GNSS Signal Detection
items.abstract: This paper proposes a phase-balanced differential Rydberg atomic quantum receiver (DRAQR) for weak-signal recovery, using local-oscillator phase control to reinforce differential signal responses and a shared squeezed-reservoir model to correlate inter-cell quantum projection noise (QPN) and photon shot noise (PSN). An analytical model incorporating QPN, PSN, intrinsic thermal noise (ITN), and inter-cell correlations quantifies signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain, outage-constrained minimum detectable power, and bit-error rate (BER) for square $M$-QAM. For the evaluated settings, SNR gain reaches approximately $10$~dB as PSN correlation approaches unity, with BER decreasing as correlation increases. Under Rician fading, at a $0$-dB threshold SNR and maximum outage probability of $0.1$, the minimum detectable power decreases from $-146.95$~dBm at $K=1.155$ to $-159.98$~dBm at $K=2.4$. Analytical results are validated against Monte-Carlo simulations over $150{,}000$ data runs per point for receiver-performance plots.
items.why: Differential Rydberg receiver model with correlated noise gives ~10 dB SNR gain for GNSS.

items.title: Optimal Fan-Out and Break-Even Routing Loss in Waveguide-Integrated Ge-on-Si SPAD Arrays
items.abstract: Splitting a waveguide mode over several Ge-on-Si single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) relieves dead-time saturation but multiplies dark counts. We quantify this trade-off with the asymptotic count-based information rate, which prices dark counts and dead time in one unit and is attained by an optimally weighted moment estimator. For a non-paralyzable pixel, the information per pre-dead-time signal event peaks at a signal rate $y^*=\sqrt{D(D+1/τ)}$ with exact efficiency $(\sqrt{1+Dτ}-\sqrt{Dτ})^2$, which sets the optimal fan-out and a critical flux above which equal splitting is optimal. We then compare four routing architectures on 64 simulated 16-pixel arrays: an equal passive tree, static trees (uncalibrated, and an idealized calibration-informed benchmark), an ideal programmable tree, and a thermo-optic Mach-Zehnder interferometer (MZI) tree with 1.32 dB excess loss. Ideal programmability gains up to 15.9 dB over equal splitting at low flux. At one known flux, however, the calibrated static splitter beats the MZI tree by 0.14-2.7 dB, and the penalty tends to twice the excess loss when dark counts dominate. In ensemble-median worst-case regret, the MZI tree breaks even only for flux windows wider than 2.55 decades, and not within six decades above about 3.4 dB excess loss. Event-level Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the count statistics and the predicted estimator variances within bootstrap confidence intervals. Sensitivity analyses cover dark-count level, heterogeneity, detector model and random seed. All results are simulations with representative literature parameters.
items.why: Information-rate analysis sets optimal fan-out for waveguide Ge-on-Si SPAD arrays.

items.title: On Random Purifications of Isometries and Channels
items.abstract: Acorn tricks turn weak quantum resources into stronger "randomized" ones. A recent example is the random purification channel, which turns $t$ copies of a mixed state into $t$ copies of a random purification. We ask whether analogous techniques can turn queries to an isometry into queries to a random unitary completion, or queries to a quantum channel into queries to a random isometry dilation. For an isometry from dimension $N$ to dimension $M$, we give an efficient, stateful simulator for $T$ sequential, forward queries to a fixed Haar random unitary completion. It uses at most one forward isometry query per simulated call, with total trace-distance error $O(T\sqrt{N/(M-T)})$. This lifts isometry query lower bounds to arbitrary unitary completions, and copy complexity lower bounds to forward access to state preparation unitaries, with dimension-dependent loss that can be made arbitrarily small for most applications. Conversely, we construct two distributions on quantum channels distinguishable exactly with two queries to an arbitrary dilation, but requiring exponentially many channel queries for nonnegligible advantage. This rules out efficient simulation of random channel dilations. Our technique also shows that approximating the quantum switch to any constant error below $1/2$ requires exponentially many channel queries, even for identical channels, giving an exponential query advantage for indefinite causal order and improving on Bavaresco et al. (2025). Finally, we show how to "decontrol" controlled forward access to an isometry: any algorithm making controlled queries to $φV$ for a random phase $φ$ can be transformed into one using the same number of uncontrolled forward queries to $V$, generalizing the analogous result for unitaries.
items.why: Efficient simulator for queries to a random unitary completion of an isometry; channels resist the analog.

eli5.plain: They show how to fake access to a random completion of a quantum map from access to the map.
eli5.how: A stateful simulator answers sequential queries with small trace-distance error.
eli5.matters: Mainly a quantum-complexity tool.
eli5.caveat: No physical reading for foundations.

items.title: Nano-Nb Superconducting 3D Josephson Junctions Arrays in Cu-Normal Matrix: Superconducting Phase Coherence and Quantum Fluctuations Properties
items.abstract: We investigate the superconducting behavior, phase coherence, and quantum fluctuation properties of three-dimensional arrays of nanometric Nb Josephson junctions embedded in a normal Cu matrix ($\text{Cu-}x\text{ wt}\%\text{Nb}$, $x = 3, 5, 15,$ and $20$), with emphasis on the $5$ and $15$ compositions. Magnetic properties were measured by dc magnetization as a function of temperature and magnetic field using a SQUID magnetometer and by ac susceptibility. Transport properties, including magnetoresistance, $V(I)$ curves, and the critical current $I_c(H,T)$, were measured at fields up to $90\text{ kOe}$. A micro-Hall sensor with ten transverse voltage bridges ($5.0 \times 0.2 \times 0.01\text{ }μ\text{m}^3$) was used to calibrate the magnetic field actually applied to the sample. Magnetization and transport measurements reveal a double superconducting transition that depends on the applied field and current: $T_c(H)$, with $T_c(0) = 8.2\text{ K}$, is associated with the intragranular response of the Nb grains, whereas the lower $T_c(H)$ is associated with Josephson coupling between grains through the Cu matrix. The response combines that of bulk Nb with signatures of weakly coupled grains, consistent with a collection of superconducting grains embedded in a nonsuperconducting matrix. The characteristic fields $H_{c1} = 400.03\text{ Oe}$ and $H_{c2} = 15\text{ kOe}$ (grains), and $H_{c1j} = 99.93\text{ Oe}$ and $H_{c2j} = 199.25\text{ Oe}$ (intergranular coupling), were determined. The critical current $I_c(H,T)$ exhibits a central maximum at low fields, followed by a long tail and small oscillations with a period of $ΔH \approx 24\text{ Oe}$, attributed to quantum interference between coupled grains. At higher fields, magnetic flux gradients destroy phase coherence and randomize the phase $θ$ of the order parameter $ψ= |ψ|e^{iθ}$, suppressing the oscillations.
items.why: Nb nanograins in Cu show double superconducting transitions from intragrain and Josephson coupling.

items.title: Nonuniform Time-bins for Making Raw QRNG Outputs Uniform
items.abstract: Random numbers play a vital role in scientific simulations and cryptography. Both randomness and security are critical requirements for random number generators (RNGs). However, classical RNGs often rely on mathematical assumptions that can compromise security, while quantum RNGs (QRNGs) face challenges, including non-uniform output due to the lack of specialized single-photon sources. In this work, we propose a QRNG model that generates uniformly distributed random numbers using a standard coherent photon source, without requiring heavy attenuation or post-processing. Although the raw data is theoretically free of bias, post-processing, if any, may be required to suppress any classical noise and device imperfections. The proposed method analytically equalizes the output probabilities under the assumed photon-arrival-time model, potentially reducing the need for heavy attenuation and post-processing to correct binning bias. We evaluate the method using real photon-detection timestamps and compare its statistical performance with conventional uniform time binning using the NIST, Dieharder, and ENT test suites. The results demonstrate improved statistical performance for the proposed binning scheme under the tested conditions.
items.why: Nonuniform time bins equalise QRNG output probabilities from a coherent source.

items.title: Quantum Relative Entropy and Information Flux Resolve Wavefunction Collapse in Spacelike-Separated QED Waveguides
items.abstract: Resolving how first-order quantum coherence and definite measurement outcomes emerge from entangled vacuum fluctuations across spacelike-separated regions is unified here by the principle that quantum relative entropy governs the energy-information flux across causal boundaries [P.~Dorau and A.~Much, Phys.~Rev.~Lett.~\textbf{136}, 091602 (2026)]. We establish the exact quantum-optical realization of this principle using dual, spacelike-separated entangled nonlinear biphoton sources implemented in quantum electrodynamics waveguides pumped by an optical frequency comb and seeded by a continuous-wave laser in a coherent state $|α\rangle$. We demonstrate that single-photon-added coherent states (SPACS) generated via coherent seeding possess a quantum relative entropy that precisely quantifies the entanglement deficit between signal and idler fields. Tracing over the unmeasured idler continuum yields an exact spatial Lindblad master equation along the propagation axis, proving that spatial dephasing is driven by an information divergence flux determined by the SPACS overlap fidelity $F = |α|^2/(1+|α|^2)$. Uniting this relative-entropy flow with quotient measurement theory (detailed in Section~S3 of the Supplemental Material), we rigorously resolve nonlocal wavefunction collapse into local coset projections---explaining macroscopic state reduction without superluminal signaling. This exact open-system framework simultaneously saturates the wave-particle-entanglement triality [T.~H.~Yoon and M.~Cho, Sci.~Adv.~\textbf{7}, eabi9268 (2021)] and anchors hardware-native time--frequency Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill stabilizers to the comb symplectic structure.
items.why: Claims quantum relative entropy explains collapse in spacelike-separated biphoton waveguides.

items.title: Decoy-state quantum key distribution with a leaky Mach-Zehnder receiver
items.abstract: We prove the security of phase-encoded decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution for a Mach-Zehnder receiver with imbalanced beam splitters and two threshold detectors that leak fine-grained information about the detection patterns. For this, we derive a lower bound on Bob's single-photon contributions and combine it with the decoy-state method and a recent phase-error framework for leaky receivers. The leakage-induced correction to the phase-error rate is independent of channel loss, providing a loss-tolerant treatment of receiver leakage even in the presence of beam-splitter imbalance. Our results provide a practical route toward loss-tolerant security proofs for imperfect QKD receivers in the presence of receiver leakage.
items.why: Loss-tolerant decoy-BB84 security proof for an imbalanced leaky Mach-Zehnder receiver.

items.title: A Theory of Partial Truth for Scientific Statements
items.abstract: Scientific representations often combine accurate and inaccurate components, which a single bivalent classification does not distinguish. This paper develops a restricted formal framework for estimating partial factual truth. For fixed content and valuation criteria, the target is adequacy to the facts, independent of the available evidence; its numerical assessment through evidence remains fallible. Quantitative claims are evaluated by normalized discrepancies between asserted and empirically supported values. Admissible finite conjunctions are assessed over a fixed basis of distinct elementary claims using arithmetic or relevance-weighted means. The resulting valuations preserve the contributions from accurate components and are independent of grouping when component counts or total weights are retained. Zero-relevance additions leave the contextual valuation unchanged, but compensation remains possible among components with positive relevance. Worked examples examine admissibility, changes of granularity, measurement indeterminacy, and sensitivity of comparisons to discrepancy scales and relevance weights. An astrophysical application connects the assessment to published observations. The framework applies to selected testable consequences of models and theories, without providing a numerical calculus for arbitrary formulas or a unique method for choosing scales and weights. It permits conditional comparisons of factual adequacy while distinguishing them from confidence, empirical coverage, and convergence toward a complete truth.
items.why: Formal framework scores partial factual truth of scientific statements by normalised discrepancies.

eli5.plain: He proposes a way to grade how true a partly correct scientific claim is.
eli5.how: Each claim's error is normalised and averaged across elementary claims.
eli5.matters: Philosophy of science; nothing quantum.
eli5.caveat: Weights and scales remain subjective.

items.title: Field-aligned measurement removes the anisotropy barrier of sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction
items.abstract: Sample-based quantum subspace methods construct a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. We study these methods for heat conduction in magnetized plasmas, where the anisotropy $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp$ reaches $10^8$ to $10^{10}$. We prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. First, if the measurement basis is aligned with the flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by $\|r_0\|_{L^+}(χ_\parallel-χ_\perp)^{-1/2}$, where the numerator does not depend on $χ_\parallel$. The bound is sharp, so the accuracy improves as the anisotropy grows. Second, in the computational basis, a subspace that misses a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as $χ_\parallel^{-1/2}$, which gives an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. We verify both results on a shaped cross-section and on a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits. At $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp=10^9$, the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives $1.3\times10^{-5}$. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of $7.0\times10^{-6}$ with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to $1.2\times10^4$ shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.
items.why: Field-aligned measurement bases bound sample-based subspace solver errors for anisotropic plasma heat conduction.

items.title: Shapiro spikes in driven quantum fluids
items.abstract: Periodic driving of a Josephson junction produces resonant transport signatures known as Shapiro spikes, conventionally described by effective circuit models. Here, we demonstrate Shapiro spikes in a neutral quantum fluid using simulations of a potential-biased atomic Josephson junction. The dc-current resonances follow the expected Bessel-function scaling, including the suppression and revival of individual resonances with increasing modulation strength. We uncover their microscopic mechanism by showing that the phase-winding frequency develops finite plateaus at integer multiples of the drive frequency. These phase-locked states are sustained by quantized-vortex nucleation and the associated $2π$ phase slips. Remarkably, within a locking plateau, the dc current and density transfer can reverse direction while the phase-winding frequency remains locked to the drive, giving rise to negative-mobility transport. Our results establish a microscopic link between vortex-mediated phase slips, Shapiro resonances, and anomalous transport in a neutral quantum fluid, revealing how quantized vortices convert resonant transport into phase-locked dynamics with negative mobility.
items.why: Simulated atomic Josephson junction shows Shapiro spikes driven by vortex phase slips.

items.title: Dynamical Signatures of Selective Gap Closing in Multi-Dimensional Monotone Quasiperiodic Operators
items.abstract: We translate the spectral gap-closing criterion for multi-dimensional monotone quasiperiodic Schrödinger operators into a concrete dynamical protocol and verify it by large-scale numerics. For a non-principal label we construct a sampling function whose leading eigenfunction weight at the origin vanishes; a local bump then drives the residual weight through zero. The height of a weighted oscillatory time average of the origin-to-localization-center correlator exhibits a deep minimum precisely at the closing, while the site-control label remains featureless and orders of magnitude larger. The signature is robust and maps directly onto superconducting-circuit and photonic platforms.
items.why: Dynamical protocol detects selective gap closing in quasiperiodic operators numerically.

items.title: 3D Printed Monolithic Optomechanical Chassis for an Unbalanced Field-Widened Interferometer
items.abstract: Additive manufacturing is increasingly being explored as an approach for producing complex structures for optical hardware. In this work, we present a fully monolithic optomechanical chassis fabricated using laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. The structure was fabricated from thermally stable Invar36, a low-thermal-expansion alloy that enables high dimensional stability under varying environmental conditions. Our monolithic design incorporates embedded optical mounts, flexures, and alignment features directly into the chassis geometry that exceed the practical limits of conventional subtractive manufacturing. By integrating the optomechanical support structure into a single compact unit, the system achieves a reduced footprint compared to traditional optomechanical assemblies. The results demonstrate the potential of additive manufacturing to produce lightweight, and highly customized optical systems, opening the possibility of new pathways for next-generation quantum sensors and optical instrumentation.
items.why: Additively manufactured Invar monolithic chassis for a field-widened interferometer.

items.title: A plug-and-play platform for self-aligning 3D-printed structures on optical fibers
items.abstract: Two-photon polymerization 3D printing advances optical fibers into complex lab-on-fiber devices. However, widespread adoption remains bottlenecked by the inherent inefficiencies of sequential, direct-on-fiber printing. To address this, a custom-designed modular platform and a corresponding fiber-decoupled fabrication methodology on planar substrates are presented. This platform features a compliant, spring-like socket that enables passive self-alignment and reversible fiber insertion, paired with a customizable frontal device. The shift to fabrication on planar substrates enables parallel batch processing and allows the substrate to serve as a functional magazine for device mounting. To demonstrate this approach, modular platforms featuring a functional tip are printed, sharpened via post-process plasma etching, metallized, and equipped with an optical aperture using focused ion beam milling, while remaining on the planar substrate. Subsequently, these are used as exchangeable scanning probe microscopy tips mounted in situ within a scanning electron microscope. Simultaneous three-channel correlative imaging (atomic force microscopy topography, secondary electron, and cathodoluminescence) is used to validate the optomechanical stability of the design. Ultimately, by decoupling the delicate optical device's lifespan from the optical fiber, this architecture transforms lab-on-fiber tools into scalable, seamlessly replaceable consumables, offering a highly adaptable pathway for broader applications in photonics, sensing, and microscopy.
items.why: Self-aligning 3D-printed fiber-tip platform for batch fabrication.
